To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the acute and early delayed effects of WBRT in patients with lung cancer are usually mild and inconsequential; however, late complications may be progressive, irreversible, have a profound effect upon QOL, and are often difficult to manage; the use of hippocampal-spare WBRT, neuroprotection, and dose fractionation may reduce the incidence and/or severity of late WBRT toxicity.
the acute and early complications of WBRT are mild, whereas the late complications may be progressive, irreversible, have a significant effect on neurocognition, and compromise QOL.

the treatment of brain metastases in lung cancer patients should be based on the following: (1) the number, location, and size of brain metastases; (2) the patient's performance status; (3) the presence or absence of extracranial disease; and (4) whether the brain metastases are the patient's initial presentation or are recurrent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel methods of brain irradiation that will preserve neurocognitive function, minimize toxicity, and improve QOL in the treatment of lung cancer patients.
the prevention of neurocognitive dysfunction in patients with brain metastases.
the late complications of brain irradiation and the development of new strategies to minimize these complications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the late complications of whole brain radiation can be minimized, and the benefits of WBRT can be maximized by careful patient selection and appropriate radiation dose fractionation.
the late effects of WBRT can be mitigated by careful attention to dose and fractionation parameters, avoidance of concominant chemotherapy, and possibly by neuroprotective agents.
WBRT remains an effective treatment for patients with multiple brain or leptomeningeal metastases and is an essential component of treatment for those patients undergoing PCI.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
WBRT should be considered the standard of care in all cases of brain metastases.
WBRT remains an important treatment modality for brain metastases in lung cancer.
the late neurocognitive complications of WBRT are real and can be mitigated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the late effects of WBRT can be minimized, but the best methods to accomplish this are still being defined.
the neurotoxicity of WBRT is not inevitable, and that it is possible to reduce the incidence and severity of late neurocognitive complications without compromising efficacy.
, in patients undergoing WBRT, there are several strategies that can be used to minimize the risk of neurocognitive decline.
